saint.name: St. John Maximovitch of Shanghai and San Francisco
saint.summary: In 1934 a young monk in Belgrade told a woman he knew that the bishops had made a mistake. They wanted another John, he said. The next day he knew: they meant him, and they were sending him to Shanghai, where 50,000 Russian refugees lived. He could not speak clearly. He slept an hour or two a night, sitting up or bowed in prayer, and never in a bed. For thirty-two years he followed the exiles, from Shanghai to a Philippine refugee camp, the United States Senate, Paris, and a courtroom in San Francisco. Twenty-seven years after his death three bishops opened his tomb at night. This is Saint John Maximovitch, wonderworker of the Russian emigration.
saint.biography:
In the spring of 1934 a young monk was called from the south of Yugoslavia to Belgrade. He taught at a seminary in Bitol, and his students had noticed that he never slept in a bed. On a Belgrade streetcar he met a woman he knew and told her the bishops had made a mistake. They wanted another monk named John, he said. The next day he saw her again. “The mistake was bigger than I thought,” he told her. “They did mean me.” They meant to make him a bishop and send him to China. He objected that he could not even speak clearly, and they answered that the Prophet Moses had the same trouble.

They sent him to Shanghai, where about fifty thousand Russians lived as refugees. For the next thirty-two years he went wherever the exiles went. He served the Divine Liturgy every day, and he lived on one meal a day and never slept in a bed. In Shanghai he gathered orphans. He worked to bring five thousand people out of China, and he argued their case before the United States Senate. In France and the Netherlands he served the Orthodox in their own languages, and at the end he finished a cathedral in San Francisco. The Russian Church Abroad glorified him as a saint in 1994, and the Church in Moscow followed in 2008. He is known as Saint John the Wonderworker.

He was born Michael Maximovitch, and he said later that he had wanted to serve justice and truth from the first days he was aware of himself. Three things stood in his way: his own body, his own tongue, and his own sense that he was not worthy. The story of how he came through all three begins in a village in the east of Ukraine.

Saint John Grows Up in a Noble Family

Saint John was born on 4 June 1896 at Adamovka in the province of Kharkov, in what is now Ukraine. His father Boris was the marshal of the nobility for the district, the leader whom the local noble families elected. His mother was Glafira. The family named the boy after the Archangel Michael and called him Misha. He was a sickly child who ate little. He loved animals, dogs most of all, and he kept away from noisy games. People often found him lost in thought.

Saint John dressed his toy soldiers as monks and turned his toy forts into monasteries. He collected icons and books about religion and history, and he read the lives of the saints more than anything else. Then he told the stories to his brothers and his sister. The family spent its summers on an estate about twelve kilometers from the Svyatogorsk monastery on the Donets river, and his parents often stayed at the monastery.

At eleven he was sent to the cadet school at Poltava. The Life printed for his glorification says he was quiet and religious and looked very little like a soldier. In 1909 the city marked two hundred years since the Battle of Poltava, and the cadets marched through the streets. The parade passed the cathedral, and Saint John turned toward it and crossed himself. Another account adds that he alone took off his cap.

The other boys mocked him for a long time afterward, and the officers charged him with a breach of order and punished him. Then someone of higher rank stepped in. One account says it was Grand Duke Konstantin Konstantinovich, and that he turned the punishment into a written commendation for the boy’s healthy religious feeling. Another says an inspector general told the whole corps that the boy had been wrong but had done well anyway. The Life says the mockery turned to respect. He had not hidden his faith, and it had cost him something. He was thirteen.

Two years later his French governess was baptized into the Orthodox Church. She had been a Catholic, and the Life says she came to the Orthodox faith through the boy’s example and his prayers.

When he finished cadet school in 1914 he wanted to enter the Theological Academy in Kiev, but his parents insisted that he study law. He obeyed them and went to the University of Kharkov.

Saint John Studies Law and Finds His Teacher

In the same year a new archbishop came to Kharkov. His name was Anthony Khrapovitsky. Archbishop Anthony noticed the student and took the trouble to get to know him, and from then on he guided the young man’s spiritual life. Saint John went to the archbishop’s monastery and church more than he went to his lectures, and he read the lives of the saints instead of his law books. He still did well in his studies. Other students called religion old women’s tales, and he answered them with the wisdom of the saints.

His Life points to one more thing in Kharkov. Under one of its churches lay Archbishop Saint Meletius, who had died in 1841. The Life calls him an ascetic, which means a man who gives up comfort for a hard life of prayer. It says that he did not sleep and that he foretold his own death. At his tomb people constantly had prayers for the dead sung. The Life says the same came true for Saint John.

When he became a bishop twenty years later, Saint John looked back at those years in Kharkov. By then Anthony was a Metropolitan, a rank above archbishop.

“The day I finished secondary school was the day a new bishop took over the city where I was to study. He was Archbishop Anthony of Kharkov, later Metropolitan of Kiev, and he became my guide in spiritual life for good. While I studied worldly sciences, I went deeper into the science of sciences, the spiritual life. The monastery where the archbishop lived, and the church, drew me more than the place where I studied the highest worldly sciences.”

— Saint John, address at his naming as Bishop of Shanghai, Belgrade, 1934

Then the revolution came, and the Russian state collapsed. Saint John took his law degree in 1918 and served in the provincial court under two governments in turn, first Hetman Skoropadsky’s and then Denikin’s. Hetman was an old Ukrainian title for a military leader. He said later that the collapse of the state convinced him to give himself to God alone. In November 1920 he was evacuated from the Crimea to Constantinople, and the next year he reached Serbia with his parents and his brothers.

Saint John Becomes a Monk in Exile

In Belgrade he entered the theology faculty of the university in 1921 and paid his way by selling newspapers. A fellow student named Nicholas Zernov remembered him from those years as a heavy young man with thick shoulders and a reddish mustache. Saint John came late to lectures through the mud in a thick fur coat and old boots, with a greasy notebook in his hand. Then he would fall asleep in the lecture, wake, and start writing again.

His old teacher had left Russia too. The Russian bishops in exile had formed their own Church, the Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia, and Anthony was now a Metropolitan living in Serbia. In 1924 he made Saint John a reader at the Russian church in Belgrade. A reader is the first rank of church service, and he reads the Scriptures aloud at services. Saint John finished his theology studies in October 1925 and then taught religion at a state school in the town of Velika Kikinda.

In 1926 Metropolitan Anthony made him a monk at the Milkovo monastery, on the feast of the Entrance of the Theotokos into the Temple. Theotokos is the Church’s Greek name for the Mother of God, the Virgin Mary. He took the name John in honor of a relative of the family, Saint John of Tobolsk, whom the Church had glorified only ten years before. That same year he was made a deacon and then a priest. A monk who is also a priest is called a hieromonk.

He wrote to the schoolchildren he had taught. In a letter of 1927 he told them not to skip church now that he was no longer there to watch them. He also gave them a rule: “Remember: Whoever quarrels consoles the devil, and whoever makes peace with others helps Christ and will be accepted into the Heavenly Kingdom.”

In the late 1920s the Serbian Church sent him to teach at its seminary in Bitol, in the south of the country. The seminary was named for Saint John the Theologian and had four or five hundred students. There he taught pastoral theology and church history. He also wrote articles against a new teaching called Sophiology, which the theologian Sergius Bulgakov was spreading. But it was the nights that the students remembered.

They saw that their teacher stayed up after everyone else was in bed. At night he walked through the dormitories, picked up fallen blankets, covered the boys again, and made the sign of the cross over them. Later they learned that he hardly slept at all, and never in a bed. He slept an hour or two, sitting up or bent over on the floor in prayer before the icons. He knew every student and what each one needed, and he blessed them whenever he came into a room or left it. One of those students remembered it this way.

“Father John loved us all, and we loved him. … Every night, like a guardian angel, he looked after us. He fixed one boy’s pillow and another boy’s blanket.”

— A student of the Bitol seminary, in the Life printed for the glorification, 1994

Bishop Saint Nikolai Velimirovich ruled the diocese, and he told people that if they wanted to see a living saint they should go to Bitol and look at Father John. In the spring of 1934 a summons came from Belgrade.

Saint John Is Made Bishop Against His Will

A council of bishops called the Synod governed the Church Abroad. On 3 June 1934 the Synod named him Bishop of Shanghai. A week later Metropolitan Anthony consecrated him in the Russian Church of the Holy Trinity in Belgrade. Anthony was very old by then, and Saint John was the last bishop he ever consecrated. At his formal naming as bishop, Saint John gave an address. He spoke of his childhood and his wish to serve justice and truth. Then he spoke of the call that had come to him.

“I do not dare think myself worthy of this rank, knowing my sinfulness, but I am afraid to refuse it. … I know my strength is weak. Out of obedience to Church authority and my spiritual guide, I accept this choice, not for honor or power.”

— Saint John, address at his naming as Bishop of Shanghai, Belgrade, June 1934

He also said what a bishop was for: a bishop “has no personal life.” A bishop must give himself wholly to saving souls and leading them to the Kingdom of Heaven. “You cannot preach the gospel without showing love in deeds.” And a clergyman “does not dare turn into an ordinary political or public figure.” He would be tested on these words.

At the time of the consecration Metropolitan Anthony wrote to a fellow bishop, Archbishop Dimitry of Hailar, to tell him what kind of man was coming east.

“In place of myself, as my soul and my heart, I send you Bishop John. This small man, weak in body, almost like a child to look at, is a miracle of ascetic firmness and strictness in our age of general spiritual slackness.”

— Metropolitan Anthony (Khrapovitsky), letter to Archbishop Dimitry of Hailar, June 1934

Bishop Saint John reached Shanghai on 4 December 1934. It was the feast of the Entrance of the Theotokos into the Temple, the same feast on which he had become a monk. About fifty thousand Russian refugees lived in the city, and their great cathedral stood unfinished while their parishes quarreled with one another.

Saint John Gathers Lost Children in Shanghai

The new bishop was hard to understand. His speech had always been unclear, and now he had to preach to a whole city. So he found a teacher. Anna Lushnikova gave him speech lessons, and he paid her twenty dollars for each one.

Then he set about his work. He served the Divine Liturgy every day, as he would for the rest of his life. The Divine Liturgy is the Church’s chief service, and in it the faithful receive Holy Communion. When he could not serve, he still received Holy Communion.

He spent his nights mostly in prayer. When he was worn out, he would lay his head on the floor and sleep a few hours near dawn. He ate once a day, at eleven at night. In the first and last weeks of Lent he ate nothing at all. He wore sandals on his bare feet or went barefoot, because he kept giving his shoes to the poor. His vestments were the cheapest he could find.

Every day he visited the sick, the prisons, and the mental hospital outside the city. For the prisoners he served the Divine Liturgy on a rough little table. To the mentally ill he brought Holy Communion, and they received it peacefully and waited for his visits with joy. He went into the Russian schools of Shanghai to examine the children on their religion lessons. The memorial church of Saint Nicholas was finished under him in 1935, and the great cathedral was completed in his years. A hospital, homes for the old, a free canteen, and a trade school went up with his blessing. In 1936 he opened a house in Shanghai for fifteen nuns of the Peking convent.

Then there were the children. Shanghai newspapers reported that baby girls were being thrown into garbage cans and eaten by dogs. Marina Shakhmatova ran the orphanage for the bishop. Father Herman Podmoshensky heard from her what the bishop did next, and he told the story. The bishop told her to buy two bottles of Chinese vodka, and she was horrified. Then he led her at night into the slums, where she knew that adults were murdered. A drunk man in a doorway growled at them, and they heard the weak cry of a baby from a nearby trash can. The bishop held up a bottle and pointed at the can, and he offered to buy the child. The drunk took the bottle, and Shakhmatova took the child. As the story is told, the bishop walked back to the orphanage with two babies under his arms.

The orphanage of Saint Tikhon of Zadonsk began with eight children. The Orthodox Encyclopedia counts about 3,500 Russian and Chinese children who passed through it over the years. One of the girls who grew up near it was Tatiana Urusova. She lived at Saint Olga’s orphanage at the convent in Shanghai, and from the age of ten to sixteen she helped at the bishop’s services. She wrote down her memories under her married name, Tatiana Kennedy.

One Christmas a nun led the girls through the sleeping city to the cathedral after the night service, and they carried a lit Christmas star to greet the bishop. He received them in his room and shone with joy, and each girl received his blessing and a bag of sweets from the big baskets in his cell. They knitted him woolen socks, and later they saw the socks on beggars.

From the third-floor windows of the convent they watched him walk to Saint Tikhon’s in pouring rain, winter and summer. The road passed a House of Mercy, an old women’s home, and a prison. Sometimes the bells rang to tell them he had stopped at the convent on his way back. He came in soaked to the skin in his sandals, kissed the altar table and the icons, and went up the back stairs. The girls sang the Greek greeting for a bishop. He asked them about their patron saints and sometimes about the saints’ lives, and then about the Gospel of the day. He asked whether they had enough to eat. In the war years the orphanage got its soup from a public canteen, and he took a spoon and tasted the soup from the pot. The children called him Vladyka, as Russians call a bishop.

“We children felt light and joyful with Vladyka.”

— Tatiana Kennedy, memoir of the Shanghai orphanage

He could be strict, and the children knew it. But they ran to him in the street for a blessing. He rapped mischievous altar boys with his staff in play, and sometimes he bent down in the middle of a service to play with a small child. On feast days he sprinkled the Holy Water right into people’s faces, and one small girl said that he squirted them.

One Lent an altar boy named George Larin gave up his bed and his meals, and his parents asked the bishop to step in. The bishop made the boy eat sausage in the middle of Lent and told him that obedience to his mother and father came first. He told the boy to go to church as before and to do what his parents asked at home.

Olga Skopichenko told of a woman named Menshikova, who was dying of rabies. The bishop came to give her Holy Communion, and in a fit of the disease she spat out the Holy Gifts. He picked them up and took them into his own mouth. Those with him cried out that rabies was contagious, and he told them, “Nothing will happen; these are the Holy Gifts.” And nothing did happen.

In his Christmas message of 1935 he asked each of his people to bring the Lord in the manger “from our hearts some kind of good deed.” That was the gift he wanted from all of them.

In 1937 Japan invaded China, and the war reached Shanghai. Under the occupation there was a curfew, and the bishop ignored it. He walked the dangerous streets at night to reach the sick, and no one ever touched him. Two heads of the Russian Emigrant Committee were killed, and then the bishop declared himself the temporary head of the Russian colony.

When the war ended in 1945, the Russians of Shanghai faced a harder question. The Soviet army entered Manchuria, and the Russian bishops in China accepted Patriarch Alexy of Moscow as their head. But the Church Abroad stood apart from Moscow, and its head was Metropolitan Anastasy. For a time Bishop Saint John prayed for both men by name at the Divine Liturgy. In 1946 the Synod abroad made Shanghai a diocese of its own and gave it to him with twelve priests and three protodeacons. Protodeacons are senior deacons. That May he became an archbishop. The Russians of Shanghai split. About ten thousand went with the Patriarch in Moscow, and about five thousand stayed with their archbishop. Three years later the question stopped mattering, because the Russians had to flee again.

Saint John Leads His People Out of China

In 1949 the Russians of Shanghai fled for the second time in their lives. Between January and May about five thousand of them were taken to the island of Tubabao in the Philippines, where the International Refugee Organization had a camp. One count puts the number at 5,500. The camp had three churches. A refugee named Knyazev wrote a memoir, and it tells how their archbishop arrived a few days before Easter.

“Archbishop John of Shanghai came to Tubabao in a jeep. He went straight to the Cathedral of the Mother of God. … The cathedral was packed with people who honored him.”

— A. N. Knyazev, memoir, quoted in N. V. Moravsky, The Island of Tubabao, 2000

Knyazev says a prayer service and a cup of tea followed. Then the archbishop went to the church of Saint Seraphim, where the bells rang and another choir met him. After a short service there he went on to the church of the Archangel Michael, and there too the bells rang and a third choir met him. He stayed about three months. When a Russian spoke to the Filipinos of his fear of typhoons, they told him there was no reason to worry. They said the archbishop blessed the camp from four directions every night.

On 12 July 1949 he left Tubabao for Washington to ask the United States to take his people. The Senate had before it a bill that would let the Russian refugees enter the country.

He reached Washington on 6 September. A Senate committee invited him and his translator to testify on the bill. Nikolai Alexandrov translated for him and had prepared a report that the archbishop called very impressive. Senator William Knowland of California gave a report first. Then the archbishop was questioned in detail about the Russian colony in Shanghai since 1920 and about how many people were on Tubabao. He wrote that it was a very important day for their cause.

Then the bill stalled. President Truman wanted it, and a bloc of senators did not. Months passed, and he made more trips to Washington. The bill passed the Senate on Holy Thursday of 1950 and then the House, and the archbishop was especially grateful to one man.

“Senator Knowland was our best helper in the Senate… He conducted the last session like a guard standing at his post.”

— Archbishop Saint John, letters from Washington, 1949–1950, quoted by Matthew Namee

President Truman signed the amended law on 16 June 1950. His statement did not mention the archbishop or Shanghai, but it said this about the Far East.

“Special provisions are made for 10,000 war orphans from the free countries of Europe and for 4,000 European refugees who fled to the Far East to escape one form of totalitarianism and must now flee before a new tyranny.”

— President Harry S. Truman, statement on signing the bill, 16 June 1950

The historian Matthew Namee tells the story of the law through those trips to Washington. While he waited in Washington the archbishop founded a parish there and named it for Saint John the Forerunner. On 27 November 1950 the Council of Bishops gave him a new post and named him Archbishop of Western Europe. In 1951 the people of Tubabao began to leave for the United States and Australia.

Saint John Serves the Orthodox of France

He reached Paris on 21 July 1951 with the title of Archbishop of Brussels and Western Europe. He lived first at Meudon and from 1952 at Versailles, in the building of the Russian Cadet Corps. Once he had been a cadet himself. His room was on the top floor.

A parishioner named Mrs. Chertkova visited him there more than once, and she remembered the room. It held a table, an armchair, a few chairs, and a corner with icons and a lectern full of books. It had no bed, because he did not lie down to sleep. He prayed leaning on a tall stick with a cross-bar on top, or sometimes on his knees, and she thought he then slept a little on the floor. While she talked he seemed to doze, but the moment she stopped he told her to go on. He was listening.

Her parish had no priest of its own. One day a visiting priest served the evening service in forty-five minutes, when it usually took two and a half hours. The people were shocked and went to the archbishop, and they expected him to correct the man. He smiled.

“How difficult it is to please you people. I celebrate too long, and he too short!”

— Archbishop Saint John, as Mrs. Chertkova remembered it

She said he taught them not to judge. A priest in one of the Catholic churches of Paris told his young people about him too. He told them that a saint walked the streets of Paris in those days, and he called that saint Saint Jean Nus Pieds. Saint John the Barefoot.

He served the Dutch and the French in their own languages and took their small Orthodox groups under his care. For the Orthodox Church of France he consecrated its first bishop, Jean-Nectaire Kovalevsky, and ordained its second. In Madrid he ordained a Spanish priest for the mission there. And he went looking for the saints of the West. Before the Churches of Rome and the East divided, the West had its own saints: Saint Genevieve of Paris, Saint Patrick of Ireland, and many more. The archbishop collected their lives and their images and sent the Synod a long list of them, so that the Orthodox could honor them again. Some in his own Church objected.

In 1951 he sent a Christmas message to two flocks at once. One was in Western Europe, and the other had come from China to the Philippines. “Born today is He Who is our Peace!” he wrote.

He had not forgotten the orphans. The children of the Saint Tikhon orphanage had crossed the ocean too and now lived in San Francisco, and their archbishop wrote to them from France. In November 1952 he told them to make their souls ready as cradles for the Infant Christ. He spent a month with them, and in December 1953 he wrote that he had become convinced “that you can be very good when you want to be.” In February 1954 he told them to stay the children of Saint Tikhon of Zadonsk and not to be fooled by any bait or to fear dangers. He reminded them of the words carved on the sword of an old Russian prince: never give away your honor. He closed each of these letters with the words “Your loving Archbishop John.” In those same years his own parents died, his mother in 1952 and his father in 1954. They had been living in Venezuela.

In 1962 the Church called him across the ocean one more time. The Russians of San Francisco had begun a great cathedral, and the work had stopped. The Synod sent Saint John to make peace, and he arrived in San Francisco on 4 December 1962. It was the feast of the Entrance of the Theotokos into the Temple, the same feast on which he had reached Shanghai twenty-eight years before.

Saint John’s Opponents Take Him to Court

Once he arrived, money poured in and the work on the cathedral began again. But a quarrel in a parish does not end because a bishop comes, and by the spring of 1963 some of the parish leaders wanted him gone. In late April the Synod called him to New York and recalled him from San Francisco. About 700 people met at the Russian Center on Sutter Street and voted to petition for his return, and the San Francisco newspapers reported it. They also printed a petition that about a dozen parishioners had made against him. It called the archbishop “generally unstable.” It claimed that he had not checked the cathedral’s finances and that he had favored the Soviet church in Shanghai. His supporters called it lies. He himself told them to obey the Synod and not to act in haste.

Then the quarrel went to court, and the archbishop wrote his own report of it afterward. One evening after the service a court officer came up to him and handed him a complaint. Sixteen members of the parish council and their helpers had filed it. It named sixteen members of the former council, Archpriest Nicholas Dombrovsky, and the archbishop himself. The complaint charged that the former council had caused losses to the church in running its affairs. It charged the archbishop with covering up what that council had done, and with calling an election that would return its members to power. A court order forbade him to call the parish meeting or to sign contracts. The next day a judge lifted the order on the meeting, and the meeting and the election went ahead.

At a later hearing the court let him wait in its library with two bishops who stood by him, Bishop Savva and Bishop Nektary. The decision was put off. On 9 July the San Francisco Examiner printed a photograph of the archbishop in court. He wrote in his report that he had held angry crowds back. His Life says he answered the slander without complaint and without judging anyone, and his peace was not disturbed. On 13 August 1963 the Council of Bishops confirmed him in his post in San Francisco. His Church’s account tells that in the end the court cleared him and the council. But the attacks went on until he died.

He had critics inside his own Church as well, and a later Russian history lists their complaints. Some bishops thought he could not run a diocese, and they pointed to mistakes in Shanghai. Some people found his services too long, and some were angry that he let Western parishes that joined Orthodoxy keep their own calendar. Others disliked his love for the old saints of the West, and still others did not trust the mild way he treated the clergy of the Moscow Patriarchate. In 1934 he had said that a clergyman does not dare turn into a political figure, and he did not become one now. Every day he served the Divine Liturgy, as he always had.

He could still be stern. One year at the end of October a group of Russians held a Halloween ball on the night of the all-night vigil. When the vigil ended the archbishop walked into the hall with his staff. He said nothing. He made the full round of the room and left, and the next day he preached about it.

Tatiana Kennedy was grown now, with children of her own in America. She told of a night in those years when her three-year-old daughter lay in a hospital after an operation. The little girl could not sleep and cried all the time, and the nurses were afraid to go into her ward. At eleven that night the archbishop came in, a man in black with a black beard. The girl stopped crying, smiled at him, and talked to him. After he left, she slept soundly.

In 1964 his Church glorified Saint John of Kronstadt, and the archbishop helped prepare the glorification and wrote a hymn for the new saint. That year he called Saint John of Kronstadt “the incarnation of mercy,” a man who took pity on everyone and helped everyone. That same year the bishops nearly elected him head of their Church, but he put forward Bishop Saint Philaret instead and said he would withdraw if they voted for him. Saint Philaret was elected.

On 12 November 1965 he paid his last visit to the Kennedy family in Oregon. He heard the confession of each of them, and he told Tatiana to read the Gospel for ten minutes a day.

In the spring of 1966 the manager of the orphanage spoke to him about a meeting that was three years away. Saint John said that he would not be there then.

The Death of Saint John in Seattle

In May 1966 he told a woman who had known him for twelve years that he would die soon, at the end of June. It would be in Seattle rather than in San Francisco. At the end of June he went to Seattle with the Kursk Root Icon of the Mother of God. The Russian Church Abroad honors this old icon as a worker of wonders, and he went with it as it traveled. The evening before he left San Francisco he served a prayer service for a man, and then he told the man that he would not kiss the archbishop’s hand again. That was four days before the end.

On 2 July he served the Divine Liturgy in Saint Nicholas Cathedral in Seattle, and afterward he stayed alone in the altar for three hours, praying. Then he took the icon to visit some of his spiritual children who lived near the cathedral, and after that he went to his room in the parish house. Men who had once been his altar servers heard a crash and ran in. They found him dying and sat him in a chair. He gave his soul to God there, before the wonderworking icon of the Mother of God. There was little sign of pain, and he reposed in peace. He was seventy years old. It was 19 June by the Church’s calendar, and that is the day the Church keeps his memory.

His body lay in an open coffin for six days while the bishops came, and two of them drove nearly 3,000 miles from Jordanville to reach him. It was summer. Yet there was no smell of decay, and his hand stayed soft. Then they took him home to San Francisco and laid him in a crypt under the cathedral he had come to finish.

Before the glorification the crypt became a chapel. Prayers for the dead were sung there almost every day. People who asked his help read the book of Psalms, called the Psalter, over his coffin. Father Peter Perekrestov is a priest of that cathedral, and he tells what the years after were like. People began going to the tomb. At first they prayed for the archbishop, and then they began to pray to him and leave him lists of names. Perekrestov says that many miracles happened there.

Saint John’s Tomb Is Opened in 1993

Twenty-seven years passed. In May 1993 the Council of Bishops of the Church Abroad voted to glorify him as a saint, and only one bishop spoke against it. Metropolitan Vitaly led the Church then, and he said he had once held the matter back but would not oppose it now. The bishops set the date for 2 July 1994. First the Synod sent bishops to open the tomb.

On 30 September Archbishop Anthony of Western America and four helpers lifted the 400-pound lid of the sarcophagus. The first thing they saw was his bishop’s mantle, shining like new, and there was no odor. On the night of 11 October they came back. There were fifteen of them: three bishops, seven priests, three deacons, a reader, and the custodian. All had fasted that day. Some had gone to confession, and others had served the Divine Liturgy and received Holy Communion. Each bishop and priest read the Gospel over the tomb in turn. At nine in the evening they sang a service for the dead. Then Archbishop Anthony bowed to the ground and asked everyone’s forgiveness.

The metal coffin had rusted through in many places. Hieromonk Peter Lukianov had kept its key for twenty-seven years, but the rust stopped him from opening the lock. The clergy would not force it, because this was a sacred task. Archbishop Anthony began to sing the hymn “We have no other help,” and the lock opened almost at once. At ten past ten he raised the lid with trembling and the fear of God. Everyone looked first at the hands. Then he read Psalm 50 and lifted the cloth from the face. The report calls the face incorrupt, which means that it had not decayed. The skin was white and the beard whole, and the white vestments had turned green. His legs were dark, with a mark where an old wound had been. There was no sweet smell and no foul smell, only a slight smell of damp earth or rust. When they lifted the body, it was light and stiff. The report puts the moment in one line.

“After the uncovering of the face, there was an extraordinary silence.”

— Report of the Commission on the uncovering of the relics, 11 October 1993

Each of them venerated the holy relics in turn. Then Archbishop Anthony told the others that a priest’s two-year-old son was very ill. Father Yaroslav Belikow was waiting nearby with the boy, Vsevolod. They sent for him, and he carried his son down into the crypt and touched him to Saint John’s hands. Father Peter Perekrestov was in the crypt that night, and he tells what came of it. The boy was healed. Perekrestov says the boy is now completely healthy, plays college rugby, and is much taller than Perekrestov himself. They sealed the new coffin in the sarcophagus, and each of them was anointed with oil from the lamp on the tomb. At a quarter past eleven they left, thanking God for His mercy. Perekrestov says it was like a little Easter.

The glorification came on the weekend of 1 to 3 July 1994. His holy relics were moved into a wooden shrine and carried up from the crypt into the cathedral. Metropolitan Vitaly led the services with ten bishops and about 160 clergy, and three wonderworking icons of the Mother of God were brought for the feast. About 700 people received Holy Communion at the main Divine Liturgy, and a procession carried the icons around the whole block. About 2,000 sat down to the meal afterward. The Church in Russia followed later. On 24 June 2008 the Council of Bishops in Moscow glorified him for the whole Russian Church. It set his feast on 19 June by the old calendar, which is 2 July by the new.

How Saint John Changed the Orthodox Church

What did he leave behind? Start with the orphanage. The Saint Tikhon of Zadonsk orphanage began in Shanghai with eight children, and the Orthodox Encyclopedia counts about 3,500 who passed through it. It moved with its children to San Francisco, and his letters to them are still printed. Then the law. The amendment that President Truman signed on 16 June 1950 opened 4,000 places for European refugees in the Far East. The historian Matthew Namee tells the story of the law through the archbishop’s trips to Washington. While he waited he founded a parish in Washington and named it for Saint John the Forerunner.

In France he gave the Orthodox Church of France its first bishop, Jean-Nectaire Kovalevsky, and ordained its second. In December 1961 he consecrated the church of All Saints of Russia in Paris. Over his life he served in Greek, Chinese, French, Dutch, and English as well as Church Slavonic. He let Western parishes that joined Orthodoxy keep the Gregorian calendar. He sent the Synod his list of the saints of the old West, Saint Genevieve and Saint Patrick among them, and asked that the Orthodox honor them.

In San Francisco the cathedral of the Mother of God “Joy of All Who Sorrow” was finished in his years, and his holy relics rest in it. In 1964 he helped his Church glorify Saint John of Kronstadt and wrote a hymn for him. His own writings are few and short. As a young monk he wrote articles against Sophiology. Later he wrote a short book on the Orthodox veneration of the Mother of God, printed with a foreword by Father Seraphim Rose. His short history of the Church Abroad was printed in 1997. He also left letters: to schoolchildren in 1927, to his flocks at Christmas, and to the orphans in San Francisco.

Why the World Prays to Saint John

His fame grew from the people who had known him. Father Seraphim Rose and Father Herman Podmoshensky of the Saint Herman Brotherhood gathered their accounts and printed them in 1987 as Blessed John the Wonderworker. The book holds about a hundred accounts of miracles worked through his prayers. Within six years the bishops had voted, and the tomb was opened.

The Church’s service for him asks him to hasten to those who suffer. People ask for his prayers in sickness, in danger, and before a long trip. The boy Vsevolod in the crypt in 1993 was one such case, and the book of 1987 already held about a hundred more.

His holy relics have gone where his people went and further. Portions of them are kept in Spain, Serbia, Russia, and Greece. There are portions on Mount Athos and in South Korea. Others are in Bulgaria, Romania, Canada, Britain, and North Macedonia. In 2013 the Church Abroad opened a mission chapel in his name at Santa Maria in Davao del Sur. That is in the Philippines, the country that had sheltered his flock on Tubabao.

In 1934 he had told a woman he knew on a Belgrade streetcar that the bishops had made a mistake. They had meant another John. He went to Shanghai with no personal life, as he had said a bishop must. He carried that rule through a war and an exodus, through the Senate and the streets of Paris, and into a courtroom in San Francisco. Today his holy relics rest in the cathedral he was sent to finish, and people still come to him and ask for his prayers. The mistake was bigger than he thought.

A Note on the Sources

Most of what is known about Saint John comes from people who knew him, and most of it was written down after his death. The parade at Poltava rests on two accounts that differ about who stepped in. Only one retelling carries the night walk through the Shanghai slums. It is by Father Herman Podmoshensky, and the 1987 book that first printed it was not available. The meeting where he first heard of his appointment is told two ways. One account puts it on a Belgrade streetcar, and another puts it at Sremski Karlovci. The Synod met there. Both say he first called it a mistake. Many early details rest on one Life printed for the 1994 glorification, from the governess to the Grand Duke. His arrival on Tubabao rests on one memoir quoted in a Russian history, and the Orthodox Encyclopedia says he sailed there with the last group of evacuees on 4 May. Accounts written inside his own Church give the result of the 1963 lawsuit, and the newspapers of that year cover only the recall and the revolt. No court record was found. One Life counts about 1,500 orphans and the Orthodox Encyclopedia about 3,500. The commission’s report of 1993 does not say what became of the boy Vsevolod. Father Peter Perekrestov was present, and he told of the boy’s healing in a later interview. Perekrestov also remembers that the coffin lid opened after Archbishop Anthony read Psalm 50, while the signed report says the lock opened as he sang. The report notes that the white on the hands was mildew, and that after they were washed the relics were a dark bronze color.

How This Life Was Researched

This life rests on about twenty-five sources in English and Russian. Among them are his own address of 1934 in Russian, four letters to children, three Christmas messages, and his report on the 1963 lawsuit. The memories of people who knew him are here too, among them a Shanghai orphan, a Paris parishioner, and a refugee on Tubabao, quoted in a Russian history. Four San Francisco newspaper reports from 1963 are here, with President Truman’s statement of 1950. So are the report of the Church commission that opened his tomb in 1993 and the decree of the Moscow Council of 2008. The passages quoted from Russian were translated for this life.

miracles.miracles:
The Orthodox Church honors Saint John Maximovitch as a wonderworker. This list gathers the miracles his Church remembers as God’s works through his prayers, in his lifetime and at his holy relics. The people who were there told them, and they were written down by bishops and priests of his Church and in its booklets. Each account names its teller, its source, and its status.

“Recorded by his Church” means that a bishop, a priest, a booklet, or an official report of the Russian Orthodox Church Outside of Russia gave the account. “Eyewitness memoir” means that a person who saw it wrote it down under their own name. “Printed testimony” means a letter that the cathedral printed. “Popular account” means a story his people tell and his Church’s writers have set down, with no witness named. Questions of date and source are gathered in a short note at the end.

During Saint John’s life

Saint John’s swollen leg heals, Shanghai

A witness quoted in Bishop Alexander’s Life of Saint John told this story. Saint John’s leg swelled badly, and the doctors feared gangrene. They ordered him to the hospital. He refused, because he would not miss a service. The parish council pleaded with him for a long time until he agreed. He entered the Russian hospital on the morning before the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross. By six o’clock that evening he had limped to the cathedral, and he served. In a day the swelling was gone.

Status: Recorded by his Church. Told by a witness in the Life of Saint John, which prints it among his Shanghai years and gives no year.

Source: Bishop Alexander (Mileant), Life and Miracles of St. John (Maximovich) of Shanghai and San Francisco.

The Holy Gifts and a woman with rabies, Shanghai

Olga Skopichenko told this story, and many people from Shanghai confirmed it. Mrs. Menshikova was bitten by a mad dog and came down with rabies. Saint John heard of it and came to the dying woman to give her Holy Communion. Then a fit of the disease seized her, and she spat out the Holy Gifts she had just received. The Holy Gifts are the Body and Blood of Christ, and they cannot be thrown away. Saint John picked them up and put them in his own mouth. The people with him cried out that rabies was terribly contagious. He answered them calmly that nothing would happen, because these were the Holy Gifts. And nothing did happen.

Status: Recorded by his Church. Told by Olga Skopichenko in the Life of Saint John, among his Shanghai years; no year given.

Source: Bishop Alexander (Mileant), Life and Miracles of St. John (Maximovich) of Shanghai and San Francisco; John Sanidopoulos, St. John Maximovitch and the Woman Dying from Rabies.

Saint John recognizes a letter writer, Hong Kong

Lidia Liu told this story. Before she knew Saint John, she wrote to him. She asked for help for a widow with children and asked his advice on a spiritual matter of her own, and she got no answer. A year passed. Then he came to Hong Kong, and she stood in the crowd that met him at church. He turned to her and said that she was the one who had written him the letter. He had never seen her before.

Status: Recorded by his Church. Told by the eyewitness Lidia Liu in the Life of Saint John; no year given.

Source: Bishop Alexander (Mileant), Life and Miracles of St. John (Maximovich) of Shanghai and San Francisco.

Light surrounds Saint John preaching, Hong Kong

Lidia Liu also told what she saw at a church service in Hong Kong. A short prayer service called a moleben was sung. Then Saint John preached from a lectern. She stood beside her mother, and they both saw a light around him about a foot wide. It reached down to the lectern and lasted a long time. When the sermon ended she told a friend what they had seen, and the friend answered that many of the faithful had seen it. Lidia’s husband stood a little way off and saw it too.

Status: Recorded by his Church. Told by Lidia Liu in the Life of Saint John; no year given.

Source: Bishop Alexander (Mileant), Life and Miracles of St. John (Maximovich) of Shanghai and San Francisco.

A tulip-shaped flame enters the chalice, 1939

Bishop Alexander’s Life of Saint John tells of a woman of his flock who began to lose her faith in 1939 after many hardships. One day she came into church while Saint John was serving the Divine Liturgy, the Church’s chief service. At the moment when the bread and wine are consecrated, she saw a small flame come down into the chalice, the cup of Holy Communion. It had the shape of a large tulip. After this her faith returned, and she began to repent of her faint-heartedness.

Status: Recorded by his Church, in the Life of Saint John. The woman is not named, and the Life gives no place.

Source: Bishop Alexander (Mileant), Life and Miracles of St. John (Maximovich) of Shanghai and San Francisco.

Saint John foretells a death, Shanghai hospital

Bishop Alexander’s Life of Saint John tells that Saint John was once asked to give Holy Communion to a dying man in a Russian hospital in Shanghai. He took another priest with him. When he arrived he saw a cheerful young man in his twenties who was playing a harmonica. The young man was to go home the next day. Saint John called him over and said that he wanted to give him Communion right then. The young man confessed his sins at once and received Holy Communion. The priest asked why Saint John had stopped with a healthy young man instead of going to the dying one. Saint John answered that the young man would die that night. The other man was seriously ill, but he would live many years. It happened just as he said.

Status: Recorded by his Church, in the Life of Saint John. The priest who went with him is the witness; neither man is named, and no year is given.

Source: Bishop Alexander (Mileant), Life and Miracles of St. John (Maximovich) of Shanghai and San Francisco.

A skull fracture patient survives, Shanghai

The Life of Saint John tells that L. D. Sadkovskaya loved horse racing. One day she was thrown from her horse. She hit her head on a rock and lost consciousness. The doctors found her skull broken in places, and pieces of bone pressed on the brain. Her pulse was almost gone. They said she would not live until morning, and that she would die on the table if they operated. Her sister heard all this and ran to Saint John in despair. She begged him to save her sister, and he agreed. He came to the hospital and asked everyone to leave the room. Then he prayed there for about two hours. After that he called the chief doctor and asked him to examine her again. Her pulse was normal. The doctor agreed to operate at once, but only with Saint John present. The operation succeeded. She woke, asked for a drink, and lived a normal life for many years. The Life counts this among the many miracles worked by his prayers.

Status: Recorded by his Church. The Life says the case was written down in the archives of the County Hospital in Shanghai; no year given.

Source: Bishop Alexander (Mileant), Life and Miracles of St. John (Maximovich) of Shanghai and San Francisco.

A seven-year-old girl survives a twisted bowel

The 1994 booklet of the Russian Orthodox Church Outside of Russia tells of a seven-year-old girl in an orphanage. She fell ill one night with a fever and screamed with pain. At the hospital the doctors found a twisted bowel. They told her mother that the girl was beyond help and could not survive an operation. The mother went to Saint John that night. He prayed before the altar through the night, and she prayed on her knees. In the morning he blessed her and told her that her daughter would live. The surgeon told the mother that the operation had gone well and that he had never seen such a case. The booklet says that only God could have saved her.

Status: Recorded by his Church, in the 1994 glorification booklet. Neither the girl nor her mother is named. The booklet prints the story in its section of miracles after its part on Shanghai, and it gives no year.

Source: The Solemn Glorification of St. John the Wonderworker of Shanghai in San Francisco, 19 June / 2 July 1994 (booklet of the Russian Orthodox Church Outside of Russia, in Russian; our translation).

A teacher with appendicitis sits up

The 1994 booklet tells of a former teacher at a commercial school. Doctors found his appendix badly inflamed and said he might die on the operating table. His wife asked Saint John to pray. He went to the hospital and laid his hands on the man’s head. He prayed for a long time and left. The next day a nurse told the wife that the appendix had burst in the night and that her husband was sitting up in bed.

Status: Recorded by his Church, in the 1994 booklet. The man is not named, and the booklet prints the story in its section of miracles after its part on Shanghai. It gives no year.

Source: The Solemn Glorification of St. John the Wonderworker of Shanghai in San Francisco, 19 June / 2 July 1994 (booklet of the Russian Orthodox Church Outside of Russia, in Russian; our translation).

A dying woman receives Communion and recovers

The 1994 booklet tells of a woman who lay seriously ill in a hospital and asked for Saint John. Her doctor said that she was dying and that the archbishop should not be disturbed. The next day Saint John came anyway. He told her that she was keeping him from his prayers, because it was time for him to serve the Divine Liturgy. He gave her Holy Communion and blessed her. She slept, and then she got well quickly.

Status: Recorded by his Church, in the 1994 booklet. The woman is not named, and no place or year is given.

Source: The Solemn Glorification of St. John the Wonderworker of Shanghai in San Francisco, 19 June / 2 July 1994 (booklet of the Russian Orthodox Church Outside of Russia, in Russian; our translation).

A possessed man dies at peace, Shanghai

A father told this story, and the 1994 booklet printed it. His son was possessed. He hated all sacred things, and he split icons and crosses into thin sticks. For several years the father brought him to Saint John. Saint John prayed over him with a cross or the Gospel laid on his head, and he told the father not to despair. One day the son asked to go to the mental hospital at Minkhon, outside Shanghai. He said that the Spirit of God would cleanse him there. Two days later the father was visiting him when Saint John arrived. The son ran to him and begged him to drive the evil spirit away. Saint John prayed over him and gave him Holy Communion. The son went home. The next day he received Holy Communion once more, and he died in peace.

Status: Recorded by his Church. The father’s account is printed in the 1994 booklet; neither man is named, and no year is given.

Source: The Solemn Glorification of St. John the Wonderworker of Shanghai in San Francisco, 19 June / 2 July 1994 (booklet of the Russian Orthodox Church Outside of Russia, in Russian; our translation).

Saint John walks Shanghai at night in wartime

Bishop Alexander’s Life of Saint John says that it was very dangerous to walk the streets of Shanghai at night under the Japanese occupation. Most people made sure to be home by dark. Saint John paid no attention to the danger. He went on visiting the sick and the needy at any hour of the night, and no one ever touched him. Zoya Bogdanov lived in his orphanage as a child, and she remembered the ten o’clock curfew. He came to the children late at night. He was never stopped, while other people were shot and killed. “We thought they didn’t see him,” she wrote.

Status: Recorded by his Church, with an eyewitness memoir by Zoya Bogdanov in the 2019 booklet. No dates are given.

Source: Bishop Alexander (Mileant), Life and Miracles of St. John (Maximovich) of Shanghai and San Francisco; Benevolent Memorial Fund of Saint Archbishop John, 2019, Saint John (Maximovich), Wonderworker of Shanghai and San Francisco: Memories of the Living Saint John and Testimonials.

A wounded woman receives Communion at night

The Life of Saint John tells of Anna Lushnikova, the voice teacher who taught Saint John to breathe and speak more clearly. He paid her 20 dollars at the end of each lesson. The Life says that in 1945 she was badly wounded and lay in a French hospital. One very stormy night she felt that she might die, and she asked the nurses to call Saint John so that he could give her Holy Communion. The nurses refused, because the hospital was locked at night. She kept calling on him. About eleven o’clock he appeared in her ward. She could not believe her eyes, and she asked him whether this was a dream. He smiled, prayed, and gave her Holy Communion. She grew calm and slept, and in the morning she felt cured. No one believed that he had come, because the hospital was locked tight. But the patient in the next bed said that she had seen him too, and a 20-dollar bill lay under Anna’s pillow.

Status: Recorded by his Church, in the Life of Saint John. The Life gives the year 1945 and says he was then in France; see the note at the end.

Source: Bishop Alexander (Mileant), Life and Miracles of St. John (Maximovich) of Shanghai and San Francisco.

A screaming patient receives Communion, Philippines

The 1994 booklet tells of a hospital in the Philippines, after his people had left China. Saint John heard terrible screams from far down the corridors. A nurse said they came from a hopeless patient who had been moved away because she disturbed everyone. The nurse advised him not to go because the woman smelled bad. He said that did not matter. He went to her and laid a cross on her head and prayed. Then he heard her confession and gave her Holy Communion. She stopped screaming and only moaned softly. When he came back some time later, she ran out to meet him.

Status: Recorded by his Church, in the 1994 booklet. The woman is not named, and no date is given.

Source: The Solemn Glorification of St. John the Wonderworker of Shanghai in San Francisco, 19 June / 2 July 1994 (booklet of the Russian Orthodox Church Outside of Russia, in Russian; our translation).

The Tubabao camp and the typhoons, 1949

Bishop Alexander’s Life of Saint John tells that about 5,000 refugees from China lived in a camp on the island of Tubabao in the Philippines in 1949. The island lies in the path of the seasonal typhoons. The Life says the camp stood for 27 months. In that time a typhoon threatened it only once, and that typhoon changed course and passed the island by. When a Russian spoke to the Filipinos of his fear of typhoons, they answered that there was no reason to worry. They said the archbishop blessed the camp from four directions every night. After almost everyone had left and been resettled, a terrible typhoon struck the island and destroyed the camp.

Status: Popular account, printed in the Life of Saint John; see the note at the end.

Source: Bishop Alexander (Mileant), Life and Miracles of St. John (Maximovich) of Shanghai and San Francisco; Russian Wikipedia, in Russian, Иоанн Шанхайский и Сан-Францисский.

Saint John on the White House steps

The 1994 booklet says that Saint John sat for days on the steps of the White House in Washington. It says this won permission for more than 5,000 refugees to enter the United States, and it calls the case well known. The historian Matthew Namee tells how Saint John went to Washington in September 1949 and was invited to testify before a Senate committee. Saint John came back again and again until the bill passed in 1950.

Status: Popular account, printed in the 1994 booklet with no date; see the note at the end.

Source: The Solemn Glorification of St. John the Wonderworker of Shanghai in San Francisco, 19 June / 2 July 1994 (booklet of the Russian Orthodox Church Outside of Russia, in Russian; our translation); Matthew Namee, Orthodox History, 2 July 2025, When a god visited Congress.

A skull fracture vanishes from x-rays, France

V. D. told of his brother, who lay in a hospital in France with a head wound. He said that many people knew there was no need to ask Saint John to visit someone. The Lord Himself showed Saint John where to go and to whom. An x-ray showed a large fracture of his brother’s skull, and he was in critical condition. Saint John did not know the brother, yet he found him in the hospital, prayed over him, and gave him Holy Communion. The next x-rays showed no fracture at all. The brother recovered very fast, and the doctor was dumbfounded.

Status: Recorded by his Church, in the Life of Saint John. The witness gives only his initials, and no year is given.

Source: Bishop Alexander (Mileant), Life and Miracles of St. John (Maximovich) of Shanghai and San Francisco.

Reader sees Saint John above the floor, Paris

The 1994 booklet tells of a reader named Gregory at the Church of All Saints of Russia in Paris. A reader is a man in the first rank of church service who reads the Scriptures aloud at services. Gregory had finished reading the prayers and went to the altar for instructions. Through a half-open side door he saw Saint John standing in a bright light, about 30 centimeters above the floor. The booklet adds that a nun of the Lesna convent told of the same thing.

Status: Recorded by his Church, in the 1994 booklet. The reader is named Gregory. The nun is not named, and no date is given.

Source: The Solemn Glorification of St. John the Wonderworker of Shanghai in San Francisco, 19 June / 2 July 1994 (booklet of the Russian Orthodox Church Outside of Russia, in Russian; our translation).

A painful hand heals after a letter

Anna Hodyriva told of her sister Xenia Yarovoy, who lived in Los Angeles and suffered for a long time with a painful hand. Doctors and home remedies did not help. At last she turned to Saint John and wrote to him in San Francisco. Some time went by, and the hand was healed. She began to forget the pain. Later she visited San Francisco and went to the cathedral for a service. At the end Saint John held out the cross for the people to kiss. When he saw her, he asked how her hand was. He had never seen her before.

Status: Recorded by his Church. Told by Anna Hodyriva in the Life of Saint John; no year is given for the healing. The cathedral visit fell in his San Francisco years, 1962 to 1966.

Source: Bishop Alexander (Mileant), Life and Miracles of St. John (Maximovich) of Shanghai and San Francisco.

A teenager recovers from lung surgery, San Francisco

Sergei Bogatsky came to the United States with his family in 1963, at the age of fourteen, and met Saint John at the old cathedral on Fulton Street. A few months later he entered San Francisco General Hospital with a serious illness, and three months of medicine did not help. Saint John visited him there from time to time, as he visited many sick people, and the boy looked forward to his visits. The doctors decided to remove the upper part of his left lung. His parents were very worried, and they asked Saint John for his prayers once more. He told them that everything would turn out well. Bogatsky woke from the anesthesia in intensive care and saw Saint John standing at his bedside, holding his hand and smiling. He recovered completely, and 57 years later he had never had any trouble from that illness. He writes that he has no doubt the surgery and the recovery succeeded through Saint John’s prayers to God for him, and that he will always be grateful.

Status: Eyewitness memoir, written by Sergei Bogatsky for the 2019 booklet.

Source: Benevolent Memorial Fund of Saint Archbishop John, 2019, Saint John (Maximovich), Wonderworker of Shanghai and San Francisco: Memories of the Living Saint John and Testimonials.

A woman survives a car crash

Anna S. told what happened to her sister Musia. A drunk young man drove into the door on Musia’s side of their car. A lung was punctured and a rib broken, and her face was so swollen that her eyes could not be seen. When Saint John came to her, she lifted her eyelid with her finger and saw him. She took his hand and kissed it. She could not speak, but tears of joy ran down her face. He visited her several times, and she began to improve. One day he came into the ward and said that Musia was feeling very poorly now. He closed the curtain around her bed and prayed for a long time. While he prayed, two doctors told Anna that they could not promise her sister would live until morning. Anna thanked God that her sister survived the night and was completely cured. Her family believes that Musia was saved by Saint John’s prayers.

Status: Recorded by his Church. Told by Anna S. in the Life of Saint John, among his San Francisco years; no year or city is given.

Source: Bishop Alexander (Mileant), Life and Miracles of St. John (Maximovich) of Shanghai and San Francisco.

Saint John visits an injured man, 1963

Mrs. L. Liu told how her husband was badly hurt in a car accident in San Francisco in 1963. He suffered terribly. She knew the power of Saint John’s prayers. She thought that her husband would recover if the archbishop came. But she did not dare to ask, because he had so many troubles of his own just then. Two days later Mr. T. drove Saint John to the house. Saint John stayed about five minutes, and from then on she believed that her husband would get well. Her husband passed through a sharp crisis, then began to recover, and he lived four more years. Afterward Mr. T. told her what had happened in the car. He had been driving Saint John to the airport when the archbishop told him to go to the Lius’ house. Mr. T. objected that they would miss the plane and that he could not turn around. Saint John asked him, “Can you take the life of a man upon yourself?” So Mr. T. drove him there, and Saint John was not late for his plane.

Status: Recorded by his Church. Told by Mrs. Liu in the Life of Saint John, and Mr. T. confirmed Saint John’s words.

Source: Bishop Alexander (Mileant), Life and Miracles of St. John (Maximovich) of Shanghai and San Francisco.

Saint John foretells his death in Seattle, 1966

Bishop Alexander’s Life of Saint John tells that he foretold his own death to three people. In the spring of 1966 the manager of his orphanage spoke of a meeting planned three years ahead, and Saint John said that he would not be there then. In May he told a woman who had known him for twelve years that he would die soon, at the end of June, in Seattle and not in San Francisco. On the evening before he left for Seattle he served a moleben for a man, and then he told the man that he would not kiss the archbishop’s hand again. Four days later he served the Divine Liturgy and prayed three hours in the altar. That day was 2 July 1966, and he reposed in Seattle before the wonderworking Kursk Root Icon of the Mother of God.

Status: Recorded by his Church. The woman is not named; Metropolitan Saint Philaret called her testimony worthy of complete confidence.

Source: Bishop Alexander (Mileant), Life and Miracles of St. John (Maximovich) of Shanghai and San Francisco.

After Saint John’s death

Six days in an open coffin, 1966

The 1994 booklet says that Saint John’s body lay six days in an open coffin in hot summer weather. Yet there was not the least smell of decay, and his hand stayed soft. Father Peter Perekrestov tells that the funeral in San Francisco was put off until the bishops could gather. Two of them drove three days from Jordanville, almost 3,000 miles. He says the body was not embalmed, and it showed no sign of decay before or after the funeral service.

Status: Recorded by his Church in the 1994 booklet, with the account of Father Peter Perekrestov.

Source: The Solemn Glorification of St. John the Wonderworker of Shanghai in San Francisco, 19 June / 2 July 1994 (booklet of the Russian Orthodox Church Outside of Russia, in Russian; our translation); Archpriest Peter Perekrestov, How We Opened the Relics of Saint John Maximovitch.

A student dreams of Saint John in vestments

Bishop Alexander’s Life of Saint John tells that soon after Saint John’s death his former student Father Amvrosy P. saw a dream or a vision. Saint John stood in Easter vestments, full of light and shining, and censed the cathedral. He blessed the priest and spoke one joyful word: “happy.”

Status: Recorded by his Church in the Life of Saint John, which calls it a dream or a vision. The dreamer is named by initials.

Source: Bishop Alexander (Mileant), Life and Miracles of St. John (Maximovich) of Shanghai and San Francisco.

A doubting deacon dreams of Saint John

The Life tells of Father Constantine Z., who had long been Saint John’s deacon and was now a priest. Lately he had been angry with Saint John and had begun to doubt his righteousness. Within forty days of the death, he saw Saint John in a dream. Saint John was all in light, and rays shone around his head so brightly that the priest could not look at them. His doubts were gone.

Status: Recorded by his Church, in the Life of Saint John. The dreamer is named by initials.

Source: Bishop Alexander (Mileant), Life and Miracles of St. John (Maximovich) of Shanghai and San Francisco.

An orphanage manager dreams Saint John is alive

The Life tells of a dream of M. A. Shakhmatova, the manager of his orphanage. In the dream a crowd carried Saint John in a coffin into Saint Tikhon’s Church. He came to life and stood in the royal doors of the altar, and he anointed the people. The royal doors are the central doors of the screen before the altar. He told her to tell the people that although he had died, he was alive.

Status: Recorded by his Church, in the Life of Saint John. The dreamer is named by initials.

Source: Bishop Alexander (Mileant), Life and Miracles of St. John (Maximovich) of Shanghai and San Francisco.

Pilgrims at Saint John’s tomb before 1993

Before the glorification, Saint John’s tomb under the cathedral was a place of prayer. Prayers for the dead were sung there almost every day. People who asked his help read the book of Psalms, called the Psalter, over his coffin. Father Peter Perekrestov took part in the opening of the tomb in 1993, and he tells what the years before it were like. People went to the tomb. At first they prayed for him, and then they began to pray to him and to leave him their lists of names. Perekrestov says that many miracles happened there. His veneration grew from the people up, not from the bishops down.

Status: Eyewitness memoir, from an interview. It names no single case.

Source: Archpriest Peter Perekrestov, How We Opened the Relics of Saint John Maximovitch; Bishop Alexander (Mileant), Life and Miracles of St. John (Maximovich) of Shanghai and San Francisco.

Rusted coffin lock opens as bishop sings, 1993

Three bishops signed a report dated 11 October 1993 on the opening of Saint John’s tomb in San Francisco. Fifteen clergy and helpers took part, and all had fasted that day. Some had gone to confession, and others had served the Divine Liturgy. At nine in the evening they sang a panikhida, a service for the dead. Then Archbishop Anthony bowed to the ground and asked everyone’s forgiveness. The metal coffin had rusted through in many places. Hieromonk Peter Lukianov had kept its key for 27 years, but the rust stopped him from opening the lock. A hieromonk is a monk who is also a priest. The clergy would not use force in such a sacred task. Archbishop Anthony sang the hymn “We have no other Help,” and almost at once the lock opened.

Status: Recorded by his Church, in the official commission report. Father Peter Perekrestov remembers the moment a little differently; see the note at the end.

Source: report of the commission, 1993, English reprint, Uncovering of the Relics of St. John Maximovitch; Archpriest Peter Perekrestov, How We Opened the Relics of Saint John Maximovitch.

Commission opens Saint John’s coffin, 1993

At ten past ten that night Archbishop Anthony opened the coffin with trembling and the fear of God. The face was covered, and everyone looked first at the white hands. Archbishop Anthony read Psalm 50 and lifted the cloth from the face, and all of them saw that it was incorrupt, which means that it had not decayed. The skin was white, and the beard was whole. The white vestments had turned green. Both legs were dark, with a mark where an old wound had been. There was neither a sweet nor a foul smell, only a slight smell of damp earth or rust. When the clergy lifted the body, it was light and stiff, not fragile as they had feared. The report says that after the uncovering of the face there was “an extraordinary silence.” It says that everyone felt a reverent peace, and that no one cried out in surprise or hurried. No one wanted to leave the relics, and they wanted only to stand beside them, pray, and touch them. Each of them venerated the holy relics in turn.

Status: Recorded by his Church, in the official commission report signed by Archbishop Anthony, Archbishop Laurus, and Bishop Kyrill.

Source: report of the commission, 1993, English reprint, Uncovering of the Relics of St. John Maximovitch.

A sick boy touches Saint John’s hands, 1993

The commission report says that Archbishop Anthony then told the others about the two-year-old son of a diocesan priest, Father Yaroslav Belikow. The boy was very ill, and father and son were waiting not far away to venerate the relics. They sent for Father Yaroslav, and he carried his son Vsevolod down into the crypt and touched him to Saint John’s hands. Father Peter Perekrestov was there, and he tells what came of it. The boy was healed. Perekrestov says the boy is now completely healthy, plays college rugby, and is much taller than Perekrestov himself. The clergy sealed the new coffin and left the crypt at a quarter past eleven, thanking God for His mercy.

Status: Recorded by his Church in the commission report, with the eyewitness account of Father Peter Perekrestov.

Source: report of the commission, 1993, English reprint, Uncovering of the Relics of St. John Maximovitch; Archpriest Peter Perekrestov, How We Opened the Relics of Saint John Maximovitch.

A friend’s leukemia is healed after prayer

Victor Boyton told of a friend from Russia, a Muslim, who had leukemia and was losing his sight. The doctors agreed that in three months he would be blind. Boyton put a photograph of Saint John beside his vigil lamp and began to pray for his friend every day. After a short time the friend was healed of the leukemia and began to see normally, and the eye doctors were amazed. From then on he led a normal life and read without trouble.

Status: Recorded by his Church, in the Life of Saint John. No year or place is given.

Source: Bishop Alexander (Mileant), Life and Miracles of St. John (Maximovich) of Shanghai and San Francisco.

A woman recognizes the monk of her dreams

Archpriest Stephan Pavlenko told of his brother Paul, who lived for some years in Vietnam during the war. Paul placed wounded and orphaned children in orphanages or hospitals. He grew close to a Vietnamese woman named Kim En, who also helped these children and later became his wife. He told her about the Christian faith and the lives of God’s saints. She told him that in her hardest times a monk had come to her in dreams, comforted her, and told her what to do. One Easter season Father Stephan sent his brother some books and journals. Paul showed them to Kim, and when she saw the cover of one journal she cried out that this was the monk who had appeared to her in her dreams. The cover showed a well-known photograph of Saint John. Kim was baptized into the Orthodox Church with the name Kyra.

Status: Recorded by his Church, in the Life of Saint John. No year is given.

Source: Bishop Alexander (Mileant), Life and Miracles of St. John (Maximovich) of Shanghai and San Francisco.

Healings with oil from Saint John’s lamp

The 2019 booklet printed in San Francisco tells that many letters addressed to Saint John come to the cathedral where his holy relics lie. These letters are private and are not read, and they are placed under his relics. A vigil lamp burns at the relics all the time, and every year thousands of people from all over the world ask for oil from it. The cathedral sends small bottles of it with a note that says it is olive oil from the lamp at his relics. Many people write back to tell of the help they received, and the booklet prints their letters: healings in cases of cancer, surgery, and stroke.

Status: Popular account. The booklet prints the letters and e-mails that the cathedral received.

Source: Benevolent Memorial Fund of Saint Archbishop John, 2019, Saint John (Maximovich), Wonderworker of Shanghai and San Francisco: Memories of the Living Saint John and Testimonials.

A young man’s vision clears after anointing, 2018

A writer who signed CK told this story. CK is a colleague of the young man’s father. In late October 2018 the 29-year-old son of an attorney had blinding headaches, nausea, and neck pain. The emergency room at UCSF ruled out meningitis and sent him home with pills for nausea. Then his vision began to fail. He saw double, and it grew so bad that he could barely see. A neurosurgeon’s scans showed pockets of fluid pressing on the spine and skull, and a spinal tap did not ease the pain. After almost a month, father and son were desperate. CK brought the father a vial of Saint John’s oil and an icon. The father is a Catholic, and he said that he believed in the prayers of the saints and would use it. CK told him to make the sign of the cross on his son’s forehead with the oil and ask Saint John to help. Two days after Thanksgiving the father did so. The next day his son called to say that his vision was beginning to clear, and the day after that it was fully clear. Then the son went to the neurosurgeon, who told him that he had no explanation for the change. After that the son went back to work. CK ended the letter with glory to God, who is wondrous in His saints.

Status: Printed testimony, in the 2019 booklet. CK signed with initials and a state.

Source: Benevolent Memorial Fund of Saint Archbishop John, 2019, Saint John (Maximovich), Wonderworker of Shanghai and San Francisco: Memories of the Living Saint John and Testimonials.

A note on these accounts

These accounts come from the people who knew Saint John and from his Church. A few points of date and source belong here rather than in the stories. The Life of Saint John places Anna Lushnikova’s night Communion in 1945 and says he was then in France. Other sources place him in China in 1945 and in France only from 1951. The Life says the Tubabao camp stood for 27 months and that a typhoon threatened it only once. Russian Wikipedia says Saint John himself stayed on the island about three months. We found no other record of the typhoon. The story of the White House steps rests on the 1994 booklet alone, with no date. Matthew Namee’s account of the Senate hearing of September 1949 does not mention the steps. The story of Saint John above the floor in Paris rests on the same booklet, which names the reader Gregory and not the nun. For 1966, Father Peter Perekrestov does not say that he saw the body himself. Perekrestov also remembers the night of 11 October 1993 a little differently. He says Archbishop Anthony read Psalm 50 and the lid then opened with ease. In the signed report the lock opened as he sang “We have no other Help.” The report does not say what became of the boy Vsevolod; Perekrestov told of his healing in a later interview. The report notes that the white on the hands was mildew, and that after they were washed the relics were a dark bronze color. Sergei Bogatsky had medicine and surgery, and he writes that the surgery and his recovery came through Saint John’s prayers to God. Each bottle of oil goes out with a note that says only that it is olive oil from the lamp, and the cathedral makes no other claim. The letters about the oil and the account by CK are the writers’ own testimony.

teachings.teachings:
Faith expressed in a life

In What do we mean by the word ORTHODOX?, John connects Christian identity with both belief and conduct. A name alone does not establish faithfulness: profession of Christ must be expressed in a life that honors God. He writes from an explicitly Orthodox understanding of the Church, not from the idea that doctrinal differences are immaterial. The practical challenge in the text is integrity between confession and action. Read the essay, especially its final paragraph.

The Cross as the sign of salvation

In his sermon on the Exaltation of the Cross, John describes Christ transforming an instrument of execution into the sign of salvation. He explains the Church's prayer for God's people as a request for grace and inward strengthening as well as deliverance from calamity. The endurance of the Church through persecution and conflict is central to his account: Christian hope rests in Christ, not in the apparent stability of states or worldly arrangements. Source: sermon excerpt, St John Maximovitch on The Exaltation of the Precious Cross.
